## The Source Base

**This article's primary sources are the seventy articles that precede it.** Each is read for a fixed set of facts, and each fact is taken from the article that states it, with its quotation. The 21 coding decisions made on top of the ledger carry quotations too. **The register of allocations is the compilation Andreas Parsch publishes from data the Department of Defense has released, read in full as the 539 rows of the copy he last updated on 23 August 2026**, with its officiality markup read at all three levels and its notes read for the sources of out-of-sequence numbers \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **Every register count in this article is taken from all 539 rows of that copy**, with no cut-off at this article's date, so the X-68A and X-76A rows are counted although neither was public on that date. The register lists designators allocated after 19 August 1998, the date of the official list of that year \[[DOD 4120.15-L, 1998][ref_dod_412015l_1998]\], and the 2004 edition of the official list was read for whether it dates its research rows, which it does not \[[DOD 4120.15-L, 2004][ref_dod_412015l_2004]\]. The compiler's appendix of unmanned military X vehicles was read as a second source on crew \[[Parsch, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles, Appendix 4][ref_dusrm_app4]\], and his page of missing designations and his account of the allocation process as primaries on the anomalies and the procedure \[[Missing USAF and DOD Aircraft Designations][ref_missing_mds]\] \[[Allocation of Official Aerospace Vehicle MDS Designations][ref_mds_allocation]\]. **Eleven original papers of the statistical methods the article uses were read for their definitions**, Kendall, Wilson, Fisher on the exact test, on contingency tables and on the Poisson dispersion test, Cochran, Woolf, Shannon, Pielou, Dunn and Fleiss with his colleagues. Six editions of the numbering rule, of 1962, 1994, 1997, 2005, 2014 and 2020, were read by earlier articles \[[X-67][related_post_a364_x67_slot_taken_by_xq67]\]. Four of them are cited here directly as well as through those articles \[[Air Force Regulation 66-11, 1962][ref_afr_66_11_1962]\] \[[Air Force Joint Instruction 16-401, 1994][ref_afji_16_401_1994]\] \[[Air Force Instruction 16-401, 2005][ref_afi_16_401_2005]\] \[[Department of the Air Force Instruction 16-401, 2020][ref_dafi_16_401_2020]\], and the issues of 1997 and 2014 are cited through the X-67 article that read them, the issue of 2014 being the first to refuse skipped sequences.

**The copy is later than this article's date, and the register then current was smaller.** The version current on 16 December 2025 was the compiler's update of 11 August 2025, as archived on 10 December 2025 \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, as archived on 10 December 2025][ref_mds_addendum_wb_2025_12]\]. It held 526 rows and 29 research rows, of which 21 were official, 6 carried the compiler's description cell, 2 were absent from released data and none was partly marked, and 11 of the research rows described an uncrewed vehicle. **It held neither the X-68A row nor the X-76A row**, so on this article's date the public register showed the research series ending at the X-66A, with no passed 67 and no passed block from 69 to 75. Under that version the ordering test covers 21 numbers, whose 210 pairs are 207 concordant, 1 discordant and 2 tied, for a rank correlation of 0.981, and 16 of its 20 advances equal one, the others being the skips at the X-50A, X-53A and X-59A and the backfill at the X-49A, so the numbers it shows permanently skipped are the 52 and the 58. It held 66 Q rows, 8 of them out of sequence, without the YFQ-48A, and of the founding-year numbers only the YMV-75A and the F-47, then dated to March 2025. **The single discordant pair, the recorded cause of every skip and the boundary of official wording at the X-60A are the same in both versions.** The two later research rows first appeared between 15 January and 1 February 2026, as The Register Stopped Being the Government's Voice sets out, and every statement here about the X-68A, the X-76A, the passing of 67 and of the block, the 539 rows, the 31 research rows and the 69 Q rows describes the later copy.

**The research survey holds 4,710 records drawn from the Crossref bibliographic index and NASA's Technical Reports Server**, of which 46 are hand-chosen sources read for their abstracts and 4,664 are admitted on their titles. Of the records, 1,713 are report primaries, being 36.4 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 1999**, and the dated records run from 1918 to 2026.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on NASA's Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. Of the 1,713 report primaries, 1,518 are reports-server records and 195 are Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The rule does not reach the journal and conference papers that report flight tests and analyses at first hand**, so 36.4 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand. The 46 hand-chosen sources are a different selection, being records chosen by hand and read for their abstracts as well as their titles.

### Thin Subjects

**Four subjects that this article's argument depends on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen or a slash read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the designation and naming of aerospace vehicles | designation, designations, designator, designators, nomenclature, naming together with aircraft, aerospace, military, missile, missiles, vehicle, vehicles, rocket, rockets | 3 |
| the crew of a research aircraft | manned, unmanned, crewed, uncrewed, piloted, optionally piloted together with x plane, x planes, research aircraft, research airplane, research airplanes, research vehicle, research vehicles, experimental aircraft | 25 |
| the cost of research aircraft | cost, costs together with x plane, x planes, x 1, research aircraft, research airplane, research airplanes, experimental aircraft | 4 |
| the research aircraft as a class | inventory, history, histories, lessons learned, decade together with x plane, x planes, x vehicles, research aircraft, research airplane, research airplanes | 8 |

**The designation is almost absent from its own literature.** The 3 titles are the designation and nomenclature cluster discussed above, and none of them names the United States research designation sequence.

**The crew of a research aircraft appears in the literature as a vehicle type rather than as a question.** Of the 25 titles, one compares a crewed with an uncrewed X-plane \[[Lechniak 2017][research_lechniak_2017]\], 22 others name a remotely piloted or unmanned research vehicle as the vehicle under study, and the remaining 2 concern piloted vehicles. The crewed-share result above therefore rests on the series' own record of its vehicles rather than on a published analysis.

**The cost of research aircraft has a literature only from 2015.** The 4 titles date from 2015 to 2018, and all of them are reports-server records.

**The research aircraft as a class has one inventory.** Of the 8 titles, 2 are editions of one inventory of the X designations, the later stopping at the X-50 \[[Jenkins et al. 2003][research_jenkins_landis_2003]\], and the other 6 concern single aircraft, a decade of X-vehicles or the structures of X-planes.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is research aircraft as a class and the institutions and methods around them. The 46 hand-chosen sources are read for their abstracts as well. Two records with the same title, from the same authors and the same kind of source within two years, are one document deposited twice, and only one of them is kept.

**Reviews of books, reference and definition entries and notices are not admitted, and a document deposited twice is admitted once.** An authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a chapter of a textbook are research works and are kept, and a glossary of acronyms and terms is a set of definition entries and is not.

**The excluded classes show where the vocabulary of designation and flight research collides with other fields.** Designation and nomenclature systems for alloys, refrigerants, animals, chemicals and genes are excluded, as are X-ray sources such as Cygnus X-1 that are named in the form of a designation. Studies of the Edwards Air Force Base site rather than of the flight research done there are excluded, among them its groundwater, subsidence, seismicity, flora, archaeology and environmental assessments, and so is a biography of an air marshal who shares the base's name. Reports admitted on the name of DARPA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, NASA or NACA whose work lies outside aerospace are excluded, among them work in natural language understanding, omics, network security, optics, astrobiology and ozone science and a genetics record on an allele named NACA, and so are technology demonstrators outside aerospace, such as unexploded ordnance clearance, road vehicles and command information systems. **Experiments flown in space rather than through the atmosphere are excluded**, among them heat pipes, spacecraft structures, thermal control, electric propulsion and satellites, and so are flight experiments in biology and materials science, the flight of birds and insects, and the ballistics of gun-launched ordnance. **The phrase research aircraft is excluded where it names a platform for another science**, such as an atmospheric or earth-science aircraft, because the X-planes research flight itself. Applications of uncrewed aircraft in other fields, such as forestry, surveying, mapping and environmental measurement, are excluded, and so are control-theory papers that use the planar vertical take-off aircraft as a benchmark model and prototyping in the sense of a tool for building components, software or simulation models. A laboratory's component products, such as cryocoolers, lasers and solar cells, are excluded as a judgement of scope, since neither the article's subject nor the cluster of sponsoring institutions, which holds the institutions and their research policy, extends to them. Correction, erratum and withdrawal notices, figures, tables and supplementary files of other works, subject indexes, and peer-review reports and decision letters are excluded because they are not works.

**Doubtful records are kept where their subject is propulsion tied to a flight vehicle, experiments carried on launch vehicles, the civil operations of uncrewed aircraft, ground equipment for aircraft, or the sponsoring institutions' own outreach and status records**, since those subjects lie within the survey's clusters on space access, flight research, the uncrewed turn, demonstrators and the sponsoring institutions. A few terse report titles whose subject the title does not settle are kept on the same terms.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### The Article's Own Vantage Point

**The article is dated 16 December 2025, and several of the facts it uses postdate that date.** The X-68A and X-76A rows first appeared in the public register between 15 January and 1 February 2026 \[[X-76][related_post_a367_bell_textron_x76_sprint]\], DARPA announced the X-76 on 9 March 2026, and the reason for the number 76 is known only from that announcement. The register itself is read in its copy of 23 August 2026, and the counts of the version current on this article's date are stated under The Source Base where they differ \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, as archived on 10 December 2025][ref_mds_addendum_wb_2025_12]\]. **Every statement about the X-68A, the skipped 67 and the block from 69 to 75 rests on that later copy**, as the X-67, X-68 and X-69 through X-75 articles said for themselves. **Every statement about the X-76's number, and the founding-year class it completes, rests on documents published after this article's date**, as the X-76 and X-69 through X-75 articles said for themselves. **The survey also reaches past the date**, its latest works being of 2026, among them the vertical-flight studies, NASA's presentation of RAVEN of May 2026 and the X-56A flutter workshop paper, which the review discusses as current literature for a reader of 2026 rather than as knowledge available on 16 December 2025.

### Historical Fact

The allocation dates, designations, contractors and sponsors of the register's rows, the register's notes on the X-50A, XQ-58A, XQ-67A and the other out-of-sequence drone numbers, and DARPA's statement of why it chose 76 are historical facts from primary documents. **The facts about individual aircraft are the earlier articles' and carry those articles' sources.**

### Measured From the Ledger and the Register

The counts of outcomes, design crews, keystone classes, ground-comparison verdicts and reasons for not flying are measurements over the ledger. The relation's totality, its two failures to be a function and its four failures of injectivity are measurements over the ledger and the register. The rank correlation, the pointer walk and the officiality split are measurements over the register. **Each can be recomputed from the register and the earlier articles, and none depends on a judgement made after the counting.**

### Statistical Analysis

The index of dispersion and its chi-square test, the Wilson intervals, Fisher's exact tests and the entropy of sponsorship are standard methods applied to the counts. **Their assumptions are stated where they are used**, the dispersion test assuming independent decades under a constant rate, and Fisher's test conditioning on the table's margins.

### Classification, Stated as Such

**The keystone class of each vehicle and the reason a vehicle did not fly are classifications made by one reader per article**, and the purpose result rests on them. The crewed result depends on the articles' statements and on a rule that a missile or rocket carries nobody, and it survives the most adverse assignment of the six vehicles whose crew is not stated.

### Inference

That the clusters are institutional rather than budgetary is an inference from the coincidence of the second cluster with new sponsors, and no budget series was tested against the allocation dates. **That a number announced as a message is a different object from a sequence index is an interpretation**, and the evidence for it is the change in how the reason was published, from a compiler's note in 2002 to a headline in 2026.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Who chose the numbers is known for three of them**, the X-50, whose number was requested by DARPA or by Boeing depending on the account, the F-47, whose choice released Air Force public affairs correspondence attributes to General Allvin \[[X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block]\], and the X-76, whose number DARPA announced. For the rest the record identifies the allocating office and not who asked for it. **Whether the share of vehicles built to measure has fallen cannot be settled at the size of this series.** A difference of the size observed would need about 131 vehicles in each period to be detected four times in five at the 5 percent level, against the 29 and 35 the series has.

## Out of Scope

This article does not revisit any aircraft's engineering, which the seventy articles before it did, and it does not resolve any question those articles left open. It does not survey the literature of any one aircraft's subject. It does not treat the pre-1946 designation systems, foreign research aircraft, or the research aircraft that carried NASA rather than military designations, as the first article excluded them. **It does not test the clusters against budget data**, which would need a budget series the series never assembled. **It does not make a documentary-trace count by designation**, and a reader who wants that measurement will need to curate title matches by hand rather than by query.

## Conclusion

**The X designation began as a count of instruments, and it still mostly is one.** Sixty-five of its seventy-six numbers went to a vehicle, the numbers the register can test kept their order in every case but one, and no fall in the share of vehicles built to measure something can be detected in the record. The first article's model of the research aircraft as an instrument describes about two fifths of the X vehicles across the whole series, and the record cannot show that it describes fewer of them now than it did in the 1950s.

**What changed is who is aboard, who pays, who can read the description, and how the number is chosen.** Of the X vehicles whose crew is recorded, seven in ten carried a pilot before 1990, and nearly every aircraft among them did, and since 1990 just over one in four has. The sponsors went from the Air Force and NACA to a spread of agencies and laboratories. The register stopped carrying the official description of each research aircraft after the X-60. **And the number went from being assigned to being chosen**, first quietly in 2002 for a pun on fifty-fifty, then openly for 1776, allocated in 2025 and announced in March 2026 by an agency presenting its choice as the news.

**The series ends at a test the X-69 through X-75 article set** \[[X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block]\]. The next research designation is the X-69A if the X-49 precedent governs, since a passed number was assigned to the next request in 2003, and the X-77A if the rule of 2014 and 2020 governs, since it defines the next number from the last approved one \[[X-67][related_post_a364_x67_slot_taken_by_xq67]\]. **Whichever it is will show whether the X-76 was a skip or a new ceiling**, and so whether the designation is still a count with a celebration in it, or has become a sequence of chosen symbols. Seventy-one articles ago this series opened by saying that a research aircraft is a machine built to measure one thing. **The designation that marks it turned out to measure something too**, the institutions that kept it.
